glp1-intermittent-fasting-muscle.title: Combined time-restricted feeding and resistance training enhance tirzepatide-induced improvements in adiposity and whole-body insulin sensitivity in female mice.
glp1-intermittent-fasting-muscle.summary: This mouse study (female Swiss mice with diet-induced obesity) tested tirzepatide alone or combined with time-restricted feeding (TRF) and/or resistance training over 8 weeks. Tirzepatide reduced body weight gain and feed efficiency; combining it with TRF and resistance training produced greater reductions in body weight and adiposity. Resistance training improved strength performance and increased skeletal muscle mass during tirzepatide-induced weight loss. Combined tirzepatide plus TRF improved glucose tolerance, and all interventions reduced hepatic lipid accumulation. This is an animal study and findings may not translate directly to humans.
glp1-intermittent-fasting-muscle.why: The study directly demonstrates, in an animal model, that resistance training preserves and increases skeletal muscle mass during tirzepatide-induced weight loss, while the drug-plus-exercise combination amplifies fat loss and metabolic benefits.

glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.title: Aging exacerbates muscle loss induced by semaglutide treatment in female mice
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.summary: This preprint mouse study treated 21-month-old obese C57BL/6J mice with semaglutide for 3 weeks and assessed skeletal muscle mass and strength. Semaglutide induced dose-dependent weight loss in both sexes. Lean-mass loss was substantially greater in females (8.6–8.3%) than males (2.3–6.6%), and female mice showed up to 14.2% reduction in quadriceps mass at the higher dose. Muscle force-generating capacity was not compromised in females but was reduced by 19.2% in males at the higher dose. The authors note this contrasts with findings in young mice and highlight age as a potentially important modifier. As a preprint animal study, findings require confirmation in humans.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.why: Provides preclinical evidence that aging may amplify semaglutide-induced skeletal muscle loss and functional impairment, with notable sex differences, raising questions about risk in older adults on GLP-1 therapy.

glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.title: Falls, fractures, lean mass and age with GLP-1receptor agonists and tirzepatide: meta-analysis of 162 placebo-controlled trials andage-subgroup data for adults aged 75 years orolder
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.summary: This preprint meta-analysis of 162 placebo-controlled trials (over 83,000 participants on GLP-1 RAs or tirzepatide) found that serious falls, any serious fracture, and hip/femur fracture were not increased overall, and meta-regression found no association between trial mean age and fall or fracture risk. However, within the large SELECT trial, fracture risk rose with age: at 75 years or older, hip and pelvis fractures occurred in 17 of 703 treated participants versus 4 of 663 on placebo. Lean mass fell by a mean of 2.76 kg more than placebo across 9 DXA trials, and by 4.12 kg in semaglutide or tirzepatide trials specifically. Six-minute walk distance improved by a mean of 15.2 m. Notably, no placebo-controlled trial reported grip strength, gait speed, or the Short Physical Performance Battery. This is a preprint.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.why: This is the largest systematic synthesis to date of falls, fractures, and lean-mass loss with GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide, and the age-stratified fracture signal in SELECT at 75+ years is a clinically important finding that has not previously been quantified at this scale.

glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.title: Obesity Medications in Older Adults: A Geriatrics 5Ms Framework for Safe and Patient-Centered Prescribing.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.venue: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.summary: This clinically oriented review applies the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework to guide GLP-1/GIP and related obesity medication prescribing in older adults. It highlights that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss may result in loss of lean mass, raising particular concerns for older adults already at risk of sarcopenia and frailty. The authors identify resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring as essential co-interventions, and call for age-stratified clinical trials that routinely include body composition and physical function outcomes.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.why: The paper directly addresses lean mass loss risk from GLP-1 therapies in the population most vulnerable to sarcopenia and frames resistance training, protein, and monitoring as non-negotiable components of safe prescribing.

glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.title: The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists as a treatment for obesity in older people: risks and benefits.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.venue: Current opinion in clinical nutrition and metabolic care
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.summary: This narrative review summarizes evidence on GLP-1 RA use in adults aged 65 and older. It reports that GLP-1 RAs produce clinically meaningful weight loss in older adults comparable to younger populations, along with cardiovascular benefits. Key concerns flagged include gastrointestinal intolerance, sarcopenia-related muscle loss, ophthalmologic complications, and hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Polypharmacy and age-related physiological changes may also increase drug interaction risk.
glp1-off-ramp-older-adults.why: The review explicitly identifies sarcopenia-related muscle loss as a primary safety concern when prescribing GLP-1 RAs to older adults, a population where functional consequences of lean mass loss are most severe.

ozempic-muscle-loss.title: Liraglutide Therapy and Weight Control in Adolescents with Severe Obesity: A Real-World Experience.
ozempic-muscle-loss.summary: This retrospective real-world cohort study followed 29 adolescents (ages 12–19) with severe obesity treated with liraglutide. After 3 months, lean mass percentage increased and total fat percentage decreased (both p < 0.05), alongside significant reductions in BMI-SDS, total cholesterol, fasting insulin, and insulin resistance. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common, and three patients discontinued due to intolerance. The authors note this is a small, retrospective study and call for longer prospective work.
ozempic-muscle-loss.why: The finding that lean mass percentage increased — not decreased — during liraglutide treatment in adolescents is notable for a population where muscle preservation during GLP-1-driven weight loss is a concern, though the small, retrospective design limits conclusions.

ozempic-muscle-loss.title: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial.
ozempic-muscle-loss.summary: The COURAGE phase 2 RCT (975 participants with obesity, BMI ≥30) tested antibodies blocking myostatin (trevogrumab) and activin A (garetosmab) added to semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly for 26 weeks (Part A) or 52 weeks (Part B). In Part A, the semaglutide-plus-placebo group lost 6.6% of lean mass; trevogrumab at both doses attenuated this loss, with an estimated treatment difference of +3.1% (95% CI 1.9 to [truncated]) versus placebo. The combination of trevogrumab and garetosmab was also evaluated. This is a phase 2 trial; full efficacy and safety data are pending.
ozempic-muscle-loss.why: This is the first large phase 2 RCT to quantify semaglutide-induced lean-mass loss and demonstrate that pharmacological blockade of negative muscle regulators can meaningfully attenuate it.

ozempic-muscle-loss.title: GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonism does not directly drive skeletal muscle atrophy or impair myogenesis in primary human myotubes.
ozempic-muscle-loss.summary: This cell study used primary human myotubes isolated from older adults with obesity to test whether semaglutide or GIP peptide directly causes muscle atrophy. Neither drug altered atrophy-related gene expression, the muscle cell secretome, myotube thickness, or differentiation. Semaglutide modestly reduced glycolytic ATP production and lactate secretion, but mitochondrial parameters were unaffected; GIP actually increased myotube thickness after 8 days. The authors conclude that the lean-mass loss seen clinically with these drugs is likely an indirect consequence of caloric restriction and reduced mechanical loading rather than a direct pharmacological effect on muscle.
ozempic-muscle-loss.why: This is the first primary human myotube study to directly test whether semaglutide or GIP cause muscle atrophy, and its finding that the mechanism appears indirect has important implications for whether behavioral countermeasures like resistance training and adequate protein intake could offset lean-mass loss.

ozempic-muscle-loss.title: Skeletal Muscle in Vulnerable Populations Receiving Cardiorenal-Metabolic Therapies: SGLT2 Inhibitors, Incretin-Based Therapies, and the Challenge of Precision Medicine.
ozempic-muscle-loss.summary: This narrative review critically evaluates the effects of SGLT2 inhibitors and incretin-based therapies on skeletal muscle, drawing on randomized trials, observational studies, and mechanistic investigations. It concludes that both drug classes preferentially reduce adipose tissue, with accompanying lean tissue reductions generally proportional to the magnitude of weight loss. Importantly, the review states that current evidence does not consistently demonstrate clinically meaningful impairment in muscle strength or physical performance, though it cautions that vulnerable populations — older adults, those with frailty, sarcopenia, or chronic kidney disease — remain underrepresented in trials. Practical strategies highlighted include resistance exercise, adequate protein intake, and individualized monitoring.
ozempic-muscle-loss.why: The review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the current evidence base on lean tissue changes with GLP-1 and SGLT2 therapies, directly addressing whether observed lean mass reductions translate to functional impairment and identifying who is most at risk.

glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.title: Weight, Fat Mass, and Lean Mass Changes After Bariatric Surgery and GLP-1-Based Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies (5,616 participants) compared body composition changes after metabolic/bariatric surgery versus GLP-1-based therapy at 12 months. Bariatric surgery was associated with greater total weight loss and absolute fat-mass loss than GLP-1-based therapy; greater absolute lean-mass loss accompanied the larger weight reduction with surgery, but the analysis did not establish poorer proportional lean-mass preservation for either approach. The authors note substantial heterogeneity and call for standardized comparative studies incorporating muscle strength and physical function.
glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.why: Directly quantifies absolute and proportional lean-mass loss with GLP-1-based therapy versus surgery, highlighting that absolute lean-mass loss is a real concern and that strength and function data are currently missing from the evidence base.

glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.title: More than just adipose: the impact of GLP1RA on lean tissue.
glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.venue: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology
glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.summary: This review discusses evidence that GLP-1 receptor agonists, while producing robust weight loss, also result in reductions in lean tissue including skeletal muscle and bone. It covers approaches that have been studied to mitigate these changes and identifies important areas for future research. The abstract does not provide specific numerical estimates of lean tissue loss.
glp1-muscle-loss-statistics.why: The paper is directly focused on the lean tissue and bone consequences of GLP-1 RA treatment and mitigation strategies.

ozempic-vs-mounjaro-vs-zepbound-muscle.title: Real-world effectiveness of 6-month tirzepatide therapy on body weight and composition in adults with overweight and obesity.
ozempic-vs-mounjaro-vs-zepbound-muscle.venue: Journal of diabetes and its complications
ozempic-vs-mounjaro-vs-zepbound-muscle.summary: This 24-week real-world retrospective study of 122 adults with overweight or obesity (without diabetes) receiving tirzepatide alongside a low-carbohydrate diet and tailored physical activity found mean body weight reduction of approximately 16%, with fat mass reduced by 35% and fat-free mass slightly decreased by 5%. Skeletal muscle mass was preserved (non-significant change). Metabolic parameters including HbA1c, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR also improved. The authors note the 16% weight loss at 24 weeks matched what was observed at 72 weeks in the SURMOUNT-1 trial, suggesting a comprehensive clinical approach may accelerate outcomes.
ozempic-vs-mounjaro-vs-zepbound-muscle.why: The study reports skeletal muscle mass preservation alongside substantial fat loss during tirzepatide treatment combined with diet and physical activity in a real-world setting, directly relevant to the body composition question.

creatine-and-ozempic.title: Creatine for glucagon-like peptide-1-associated muscle loss.
creatine-and-ozempic.summary: This hypothesis paper proposes that rapid weight loss and associated reductions in energy and protein intake, mechanical loading, and potentially physical activity during GLP-1-based therapy may create conditions of increased skeletal muscle bioenergetic vulnerability. The authors hypothesize that creatine supplementation could be a biologically plausible adjunct to support muscle energetics and function in this setting. The paper explicitly states this is hypothesis-generating and that no randomized clinical trial has directly evaluated creatine supplementation during GLP-1-based pharmacological weight loss.
creatine-and-ozempic.why: The paper directly frames the mechanistic rationale for a specific muscle-preservation adjunct during GLP-1 therapy, while being transparent that clinical evidence is currently absent.

glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.title: Nutrition Care Strategies at the Intersection of Menopause and Obesity Pharmacotherapy.
glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.summary: This narrative review examines nutritional risks for perimenopausal women using incretin mimetic pharmacotherapies. It identifies overlapping vulnerabilities: estrogen deficiency combined with GLP-1-driven appetite suppression, reduced energy intake, and gastrointestinal side effects that together heighten risk for sarcopenic obesity and osteoporosis. Clinical strategies discussed include protein optimization, micronutrient monitoring, menopausal hormone therapy for musculoskeletal health, and multidisciplinary care.
glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.why: Identifies perimenopausal women on GLP-1 therapy as a group with compounded risk for lean-mass and bone loss, and frames protein and micronutrient adequacy as central mitigation strategies.

glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.title: Semaglutide in postmenopausal women: Clinical implications for weight loss, muscle health, and sleep-disordered breathing.
glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.summary: This narrative mini-review examines semaglutide use in postmenopausal women, focusing on muscle health and sleep-disordered breathing. It notes that GLP-1 RA-induced weight loss is associated with decreases in lean body mass, though the functional consequences remain incompletely understood, and that reductions in lean body mass do not necessarily reflect clinically meaningful skeletal muscle loss. The review highlights that overcoming anabolic resistance through adequate protein and micronutrient intake and resistance exercise may help preserve musculoskeletal health, though evidence in semaglutide-treated postmenopausal women remains indirect.
glp1-muscle-loss-women-over-50.why: The paper addresses the intersection of GLP-1-induced lean mass changes and the heightened sarcopenia risk of postmenopause, a population where anabolic resistance makes muscle preservation particularly challenging.

signs-of-muscle-loss-glp1.title: Weaker or Just Lighter? Monitoring Strength and Function, Not Just Lean Mass, During GLP-1 Weight Loss.
signs-of-muscle-loss-glp1.summary: This narrative review argues that body-composition studies of GLP-1-based therapy report lean-mass changes but rarely measure whether patients are actually getting weaker. The review notes that in older adults, strength declines roughly three times faster than lean mass and predicts mortality where lean mass does not. A 2026 review of 35 body-composition trials found none that measured objective physical function. The authors propose a pragmatic (but explicitly unvalidated) monitoring schedule using grip strength, five-times chair-stand time, and usual gait speed at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months, with particular attention to older adults, those with low baseline strength, frailty, or rapid weight loss.
signs-of-muscle-loss-glp1.why: This review directly challenges the assumption that tracking lean mass is sufficient during GLP-1-based weight loss, proposing that functional strength measures may be a more meaningful and mortality-relevant signal.

best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.title: Effects of Anti-Diabetic Drugs on Satellite Cell Function: A Mini Review.
best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.venue: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology
best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.summary: This mini-review examines emerging evidence on whether metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors modulate satellite cell function in skeletal muscle. Satellite cells are muscle stem cells important for adaptation to stimuli such as exercise. The review notes that the mechanisms by which these drugs produce off-target effects on skeletal muscle — including potential satellite cell involvement — are not yet clear, and asks whether this represents a relevant therapeutic target.
best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.why: Understanding whether GLP-1 receptor agonists affect the muscle stem cells responsible for repair and adaptation to exercise is directly relevant to the question of how these drugs interact with resistance training outcomes.

best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.title: Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial.
best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.summary: This two-arm RCT (120 adults with overweight or obesity, 40 weeks) randomized participants to tirzepatide alone or tirzepatide plus thrice-weekly resistance exercise training. Both groups achieved similar total weight loss (~22 kg). Resistance exercise did not significantly alter fat-mass loss but significantly reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (tirzepatide alone: −4.67 kg; tirzepatide plus resistance exercise: −3.57 kg; between-group difference 1.09 kg, 95% CI 0.43–1.75 kg). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide alone but increased with the addition of resistance exercise across all three measured exercises.
best-exercises-preserve-muscle-glp1.why: This RCT provides direct, quantified evidence that resistance exercise training preserves lean mass and increases muscle strength during tirzepatide-induced weight loss, where tirzepatide alone reduced strength.

protein-on-glp1.title: Nutrition in the Era of Incretin-Based Therapies: Clinical Strategies for Optimizing Care.
protein-on-glp1.summary: This narrative review summarizes current evidence and practical nutrition strategies for patients on GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists. It identifies reduced oral intake, gastrointestinal side effects, lean mass loss, and potential micronutrient inadequacy as key concerns. The review covers individualized dietary approaches for gastrointestinal symptoms and special populations, and concludes that nutrition care is a critical component of incretin-based treatment to preserve lean body mass, optimize nutrient intake, and support long-term adherence.
protein-on-glp1.why: The paper directly addresses lean mass loss and nutritional adequacy as central management challenges during GLP-1 therapy, with practical dietary framing.

protein-on-glp1.title: Nutritional and lifestyle strategies in obesity management during incretin-based therapy: a narrative review with practical recommendations.
protein-on-glp1.summary: This narrative review, graded using Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels, synthesizes nutritional strategies for patients on GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists. It identifies adequate protein intake (cited as 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day in the abstract), body composition monitoring, resistance exercise, hydration, and micronutrient surveillance as particularly relevant pillars. The authors propose three expert-derived frameworks — the Incretin Plate Model, the Metabolic Hourglass Model, and a muscle-preservation/deficiency-screening framework — while noting these have not yet been validated.
protein-on-glp1.why: This review directly synthesizes the nutritional and exercise evidence for preserving muscle mass during incretin-based therapy and proposes structured monitoring frameworks, though the frameworks themselves await prospective validation.

protein-on-glp1.title: Structured nutritional management of insulin resistance in women with PMOS (formerly PCOS) receiving GLP-1RA therapy.
protein-on-glp1.summary: This structured review examined GLP-1 receptor agonist use in women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS, formerly PCOS). GLP-1RAs produced consistent reductions in weight, androgens, and fasting insulin, but insulin-resistance outcomes were heterogeneous and reversed after treatment withdrawal. The authors identify appetite suppression as a driver of inadequate protein intake and micronutrient depletion, and propose a three-phase clinical nutrition protocol emphasizing protein optimization, micronutrient repletion, and resistance exercise alongside GLP-1RA therapy.
protein-on-glp1.why: The review explicitly links GLP-1RA-induced appetite suppression to inadequate protein intake and lean-mass risk in a specific female population, and proposes structured nutritional and exercise countermeasures.

glp1-high-protein-meals-nausea.title: Nutritional Strategies for Managing Gastrointestinal Adverse Effects Associated with GLP-1 Receptor Agonist and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy: A Narrative Review with Practical Recommendations
glp1-high-protein-meals-nausea.summary: This preprint narrative review examines gastrointestinal adverse effects of GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists — including nausea, vomiting, constipation, and bloating — and their impact on dietary quality and nutritional adequacy. The authors present symptom-specific dietary recommendations covering meal distribution, fat and fiber intake, hydration, and food choices. A key theme is that GI side effects can compromise protein intake, increase micronutrient deficiency risk, and threaten muscle mass preservation during treatment.
glp1-high-protein-meals-nausea.why: Directly links GLP-1-induced gastrointestinal side effects to reduced protein intake and muscle-mass risk, and proposes practical nutritional strategies to mitigate these effects.

build-new-muscle-on-glp1.title: Testosterone Added to Incretin Therapy in Men With Overweight or Obesity: A Systematic Review of Body Composition Evidence and Gaps.
build-new-muscle-on-glp1.summary: This PROSPERO-registered systematic review searched seven databases for evidence on testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) added to incretin treatment in men with overweight or obesity and hypogonadism. Only two reports with very low certainty evidence were identified: a nonrandomized pilot (five men per group) showing a lean-mass difference of +2.70 kg (95% CI −1.75 to +7.15) and a randomized conference report attributing a smaller proportion of weight loss to fat-free mass with TRT versus without. No usable strength, function, or safety comparisons were found. The authors conclude that available evidence does not establish incremental TRT benefit for body composition or muscle outcomes, and that TRT solely for lean-tissue preservation is unsupported.
build-new-muscle-on-glp1.why: This is a direct, rigorously conducted systematic review of whether adding testosterone to incretin therapy preserves muscle mass — a question highly relevant to men on GLP-1 medications — and it finds the evidence base is essentially absent.

dexa-inbody-scan-glp1.title: Body Composition Monitoring in Older Adults on GLP-1 Receptor Agonists A Narrative Review of Assessment Methods
dexa-inbody-scan-glp1.summary: This preprint narrative review evaluated body composition assessment methods for monitoring older adults receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists, noting that a meaningful proportion of GLP-1-driven weight loss is lean tissue and that bone effects remain uncertain. DXA was identified as the most practical reference method but its precision declined with obesity. Bioelectrical impedance analysis was highly repeatable but accuracy varied widely between devices. Smartphone apps and 3D optical imaging were the most scalable but have not been validated in older adults or for tracking change, and none of the accessible methods measured bone. The authors conclude no current method is both valid and scalable for this population.
dexa-inbody-scan-glp1.why: This review directly addresses the practical challenge of monitoring muscle and lean mass loss in older adults on GLP-1 therapy — a core concern for this readership — and maps the limitations of available tools.

glp1-knee-osteoarthritis-pain.title: Clinical Considerations With GLP-1 Therapies for Obesity and Knee Osteoarthritis: A Focus on Musculoskeletal Health and Nutritional Concerns.
glp1-knee-osteoarthritis-pain.summary: This narrative review examines the musculoskeletal and nutritional implications of GLP-1 therapy in the context of knee osteoarthritis. It highlights that weight loss with these agents carries risks of muscle and bone loss and malnutrition, and argues that success should be judged by improvements in physical function, body composition, and musculoskeletal health rather than weight loss magnitude alone. The authors call for combining pharmacotherapy with evidence-based nutrition and exercise strategies.
glp1-knee-osteoarthritis-pain.why: The review directly addresses muscle and bone loss as inadvertent consequences of GLP-1-driven weight loss and frames exercise and nutrition as essential co-interventions.
